findings.text: The first paragraph tells a newcomer what Athena is, who it is for and what problem it solves, in plain words. This part works well.
findings.source: Athena is an open-source system, written in Rust, that turns a short request into a change to a code repository. ... It solves the problem of AI edits that arrive unreviewed and unaccountable.

findings.text: The only section that would show Athena's main promise (models, verdict, cost traced to a request) is an error message, and it is the first section after the header. A newcomer gets no proof of the claims in the opening paragraph, and the page looks broken.
findings.source: Check it on a real job: "The records of job 20261029-073603-7kqv could not be read here, so no models, verdict or costs are shown: no reading record for job 20261029-073603-7kqv."

findings.text: Someone visiting Athena's homepage lands on a long study of a different project, firstmate. The third paragraph says why (to show Athena can read and explain a project), but most of the page is about firstmate, so a newcomer may not know which tool the site is about.
findings.source: Page title and h1: "Athena explains how firstmate handles work"

findings.text: This link sits in the header with no explanation. A newcomer is not an owner and cannot tell what the proposals are or whether the link is meant for them.
findings.source: Owner view: proposals waiting for your decision

findings.text: The firstmate study is careful for a newcomer: it defines terms before using them, has a core track with an optional expert view, and walks one task from start to finish. Even so, its gates, exit codes and lock rules are heavy reading for someone who came to learn about Athena.
The glossary is honest about gaps, but five entries say the term is undefined. This leaves the newcomer with words they still cannot fully understand.
findings.source: Glossary: "The firstmate source does not define a captain call." (similar entries for durable record, endpoint, heartbeat, wake)

findings.text: The next steps are concrete: clone, check prerequisites, run setup, try one command, and the page says what that command does. The header links straight to this section, so a newcomer knows what to do next.
findings.source: Next steps: "git 2.40 or later; a C linker (cc) ... curl ... Claude Code, or npm to install it." and "Install Athena from the checkout: ./setup.sh" and "athena ask \"add a changelog\""

findings.text: The page never says whether running Athena needs an account, an API key or paid model use. That matters because the opening paragraph says Athena records what each step costs.
findings.source: Try it with a one-line request: athena ask "add a changelog" ... press Enter to run it on that repository.
